sentences.text: This predator measured between 1.5 and 2.07 meters in length and weighed roughly 14.1 to 19.7 kilograms.
It is recognized by a long, low skull featuring an upturned snout, a trait that separates it from other members of its family.
However, some researchers estimate the animal could have grown to about 2.5 meters and reached a mass of 28 kilograms.
Henry Fairfield Osborn first described the genus in 1924, naming the type species Velociraptor mongoliensis that same year.
Remains of this species were unearthed in the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia.
A second species, V. osmolskae, was identified in 2008 based on skull fragments found in the Bayan Mandahu Formation of China.
Feathers on its body likely aided in movement across slopes or were used for nest brooding and display.
Its hearing range, spanning 2,368 to 3,965 Hz, would have helped it track moving prey.
As an opportunistic hunter with an elongated snout for catching small, fast animals, it also scavenged carrion when droughts struck or health declined.
Taxonomically, it sits within Eudromaeosauria and is frequently placed in its own subfamily, Velociraptorinae.
Some scientists argue it belongs in Archaeopterygidae, suggesting it was a flightless bird.
It inhabited Asia during the Late Cretaceous epoch, specifically between 75 and 71 million years ago in the Campanian stage.
Conflicts exist regarding V. osmolskae, with some studies placing it closer to Linheraptor, while others suggest the subfamily Velociraptorinae is not a distinct group but a paraphyletic grade.
Additionally, the classification of a specific dromaeosaurid specimen from Ukhaa Tolgod remains uncertain.
